headline: Biddeford Pool at first light: bass rolling on mackerel, and my knuckles still remember it
subhead: The incoming tide at the Pool turned on like a switch this week, and Pine Point's blues are chewing anything silver.
body_markdown:
Tuesday, five-forty in the morning, still gray enough that I needed the headlamp to thread a hook, and a striper close to twenty-eight inches nearly took the rod out of my hand off the rocks at the mouth of the Pool. Second cast. That's the kind of morning that makes you forgive this stretch of coast for every skunking it's handed you in June. The fish was sitting right where the current pinches around the ledge on the incoming, holding in maybe six feet of water, and it hit a Danny plug like it meant it. Landed three more before the tide finished filling, biggest one twenty-nine inches, all of them fat and chrome and clearly fresh off a mackerel diet.

That's been the story all week down here — mackerel pushing into the river mouths and the bass following them in tight to the beach on the push. Biddeford Pool remains the best hour of striper fishing in this state when the water's coming in around the sandbar and pinning bait against the rocks. I've had my best luck starting an hour before the bottom of the low, working a big swimming plug — the Danny, a Bomber Long A in mackerel pattern, anything that throws a wide wobble — right along that rock line where the channel necks down. Slow retrieve, let it dig, don't rush it. The fish are eating with real purpose right now, not just pecking.

Pine Point's been a different animal entirely — that's where the bluefish have shown up and started tearing through peanut bunker pods right off the jetty and along the beach toward the Scarborough River mouth. Choppers in the three-to-six-pound class, occasional bigger ones mixed in, blitzing hard enough on some mornings that you can see the water churn white from fifty yards off. Bring wire or heavy fluoro leader if you don't want to donate every lure in your bag — these blues don't care what you throw as long as it's got some flash. Kastmasters, Hopkins spoons, and a bucktail with a white tube on it have all been getting hit. This lines up with what we've been tracking coastwide — the bluefish push that's been running the beaches from New Jersey up through the Sound has finally found its way into our water, and with bunker and mackerel schools still holding tight along the beachfront here, I don't expect that bite to slow down until the bait scatters or we get a real wind shift.

Higgins Beach has had flashes of the same thing but it's spottier — you'll walk into a blitz one morning and find dead water the next. The birds are the tell. If you're not seeing gulls diving, don't waste your morning standing there. Prouts Neck has been fishing well on a southwest wind, which we've had a few days of this week — that wind pushes bait against the rocks on the ocean side and the bass tuck in tight to the ledges off the point. Bucktails tipped with a strip of mackerel belly, worked slow along bottom in fifteen to twenty feet, have been the ticket there for a mixed bag of school bass and the occasional keeper.

Water temps are still running cooler than most of the coast to our south — we're sitting in the low sixties nearshore, which is exactly why this zone keeps fishing better in daylight than places from Boston south where the stripers have gone nocturnal on account of warm surface water. That cold Gulf of Maine water is a gift right now. While guys from Cape Cod down are grinding out dawn-and-dusk-only bites because the fish are pushed deep and sour on the heat, our stripers are still willing to eat mid-morning in six to fifteen feet of water. Don't sleep late this time of year — it's not required the way it is farther south.

Groundfish program has been steady but unspectacular. Flounder are still coming out of Wells Harbor and the flats around the Kennebunk River mouth on sandworms and clam bellies fished on the bottom during slower tide stages, mostly dinner-plate size with the occasional bigger one mixed in. Cod fishing offshore of Cape Elizabeth has been a grind — you need to find the right piece of structure and jig it patiently, nothing's stacked up thick, but a few decent fish in the eight-to-twelve-pound range have come over the rail on diamond jigs worked right off bottom.

Moon's waning toward the new phase this week, which means tides are building again after sitting on the smaller side — that should tighten up the current at the Pool and improve the push of bait into the estuary mouths through the weekend. If the wind stays out of the southwest like it has been, I'd fish Prouts Neck early and then slide over to the Pool for the last two hours of the incoming — that's been the most consistent one-two punch all week. If it swings onshore and kicks up surf, I'd rather be at Pine Point working the bluefish blitz than getting hammered by whitewater trying to swing a plug through the wash at the Pool. Watch the bait. Where the mackerel show, the bass aren't far behind, and right now that's most of this coastline.
